label: The paper does not indicate whether code will be shared, limiting reproducibility.
The proposed method has limited novelty.
The method’s novelty is limited because it relies mainly on techniques from the authors’ NIPS 2015 paper.
Theorem 1 lacks assumptions controlling the accuracy of \tilde{T} as an approximation to T, which may be needed for its conclusions.
The paper’s overall presentation is difficult to follow.
The paper does not clearly position its indistinguishability and training–inference mismatch issues against prior work [1,2], limiting novelty.
Section 3.1’s definition and its redefinition in Equation 2 are confusing; use distinct notation.
Equation (6) is not sufficiently explained or derived.
The paper needs more high-level intuition for how the approach works.
The experimental results are not explained sufficiently.
The notation in Equation 2 is not clearly defined.
The proof of Theorem A.2 lacks sufficient detail.
The title of Section 3.3 contains a typo.
The paper does not clearly articulate its specific contribution.
Page 7 has a typo: “change” should read “changes.”
Equation (4) appears incorrect.
Notation throughout the paper is confusing and inconsistent.
Page 2, equation (2), uses the wrong subscript: it should be p rather than ℙ.
The second paragraph of Section 3.1 is unclear and strangely worded.
The condition used in Theorem 2 needs an explanation in natural language.
The paper does not explain why GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT cannot capture the claimed node dependencies and local/global graph-structure similarities.
Section 2.2 does not clearly explain how the approach is motivated by auxiliary training.
Section 3.3 is difficult to follow and should be revised more concisely.
The paper does not clearly specify which loss the proposed procedure minimizes.
The paper lacks enough implementation detail for readers to re-implement the method.
The experimental results are not especially strong.
Section 3.2.1 does not explain the theoretical results clearly enough.
The paper does not establish how its method compares with standard data augmentation such as noise, dropout, and transformations.
The paper contains typos and grammatical errors.
Algorithm 1 is unclear and omits quantities such as L.
The last paragraph on page 1 contains a grammatical error in how its phrases are formulated.
The paper should explain its method more didactically for a machine-learning audience.
The related-work discussion omits Cai et al. (ICLR 2017).
Page 2 has a grammatical error in “learning a discriminative representations.”
The paper should relate its results to CV work, including Ivanov et al. and Ledig et al., and explain why partially conditioned models avoid degeneracy.
The contribution appears limited to applying existing algorithms to this task, with little methodological novelty.
The paper's writing needs improvement.
Equation (9)'s “L2” term is undefined, and its equivalence to maximizing Equation (8)'s first term is unexplained.
Section 3.2 does not explain the approach sufficiently.
The paper does not justify its integer-programming formulation or explain its benefits over standard gradient-based approaches.
Algorithm 2 is mentioned without enough discussion to make it clear.
The evaluation should include datasets beyond CIFAR-10.
The paper contains typos.
The phrase “a interpretable” should read “an interpretable.”
Equation (2) is unclear or potentially incorrect because it uses ∇π without defining whether it means ∇a Q(sᵢ₊₁,aᵢ₊₁) · ∇s π(sᵢ₊₁).
The paper lacks theoretical justification for why its pseudo-labeling approach works.
On CIFAR-10, proposed methods improve test accuracy but baselines achieve lower training loss, leaving relative performance unclear; the paper does not explain this discrepancy.
The derivation around Equation (6) uses ambiguous p notation for discrete labels, empirical samples, and true distributions; these should be distinguished.
Theorem 1 and Corollaries 1–2 may largely apply a known result to this setting, making their theoretical originality unclear.
The experiments do not compare the approach with existing methods.
The paper does not explain why its approach is practically superior to batch normalization for addressing deep-network training difficulties.
Equation 2 does not clarify whether X and A_t use pointwise or matrix-vector multiplication, despite their stated dimensions.
The notation beneath the sigma in Eq. 2 is incorrect; it should begin with \(\tilde{X}\in\{...\}\).
Calling the approach “contrastive” on page 2 is inaccurate because the paper has no contrastive objective.
The paper does not explain the motivation for the proposed algorithm or its formulation.
Section 3 does not clearly explain how its description relates to the proposed framework.

The assumptions in Theorems 2 and 7—orthogonal data columns, sparsity only in the first layer, and one hidden connection per input—are strong and unlikely in practice, with insufficient justification.
The paper does not address whether its methods extend beyond regression to classification.
The experiments lack comparisons with GNN models such as Xu et al. [2].
Sections 3–4 do not clearly define state s_t or provide an example, making the formulation difficult to follow.
The paper does not provide sufficient intuition for its theoretical results.
Figure 2 does not explain what its different colors depict.
The paper does not clearly explain how its method differs from Spithourakis and Riedel (2018) and related approaches.
The paper does not explain or empirically justify the feature-integration sequence of 3×3 spatial convolution, flattening L and C*F, and 1×1×1 spatio-temporal convolution.
The paper does not define the set of probability densities explicitly or establish that the setting satisfies the Hilbert-space assumptions used for Proposition 1.
The experiments need comparisons with more baselines.
The results do not substantially improve state-of-the-art performance.
The related-work discussion should cite Bayesian-approximation work, such as Gal and Ghahramani (2016).
The paper does not establish theoretically or experimentally that its simple-model analysis extends to deep nonlinear activations such as ReLU, including numerical stability.
The line containing “for improved generalization: For Unsupervised Representation Learning” needs correction or clarification.
The paper does not properly define its terminology.
Reference [2] should cite its NeurIPS version rather than its arXiv version.
The paper’s quadratic-loss approximation is only reasonable near training’s end, so it cannot characterize the full training procedure or its practical methods.
The paper lacks experiments on larger state-of-the-art networks, so it is unclear whether Table 6’s trends hold for models such as WideResNet-28x10.
Section 2's notation is unclear, including the undefined symbol k.
Assumption 3.1 is not guaranteed to hold, and the paper does not justify it.
Section 2.4 does not clearly motivate the independent-marginals setting, given that the approach seems more useful with dependent information.
The paper does not clarify how its work relates to established methods such as DANN and CDANN.
The Introduction does not sufficiently highlight or explain sparse residuals, the work’s core deviation from prior techniques.
Section 3.2 does not specify the sampling distributions for I_k and J_k or clarify whether Assumptions 4.14–4.16 supply those conditions.
The paper does not explain how the approach’s hyperparameters were chosen or tuned.
Figure 4 omits exact valid NLL values for each panel, making performance—especially between panels 2 and 3—difficult to distinguish.
Figure 2 is unclear and needs more explanation.
The paper lacks a novel, generally applicable machine-learning contribution, making its suitability for ICLR questionable.
Equations (1)–(2) do not clarify that Equation (2) is only one possible way to learn the model parameters.
The phrase “more complicated convergence” at line 203 is unclear.
The gradient expression in the unnumbered equation after (5) appears inconsistent with the gradient implied by the supplementary algorithm.
Section 5.2 provides too little analysis of how the inequality regularizers alter representations or why some work better than others.
The manuscript’s writing is confusing and difficult to follow.
Figure 4 is crowded and difficult to parse; the plots should be widened, their content reduced, and a legend added.
The experiments show only marginal improvements over competing methods.
Figure 4’s caption contains typos.
Claims that approaches are better lack evidence, including that small networks suit the data and pretraining increases training efficiency.
Excessive reliance on the appendix leaves the paper insufficiently self-contained; key results should be moved into the main body.
The paper does not explain why gradient step-size choices play no larger role in the stated results.
The SDE-based analysis may not capture SGD when its noise is non-Gaussian, making the theoretical argument weaker than Blanc et al.’s rigorous result.
Figures 3 and 4 do not clearly show that the learned filters reflect the predominant data structure.
The novelty is limited because prior depth-based adaptive-computation methods, including McGill et al., Bolukbasi et al., and Figurnov et al., readily extend to sequence models.
The paper uses inconsistent hyphenation, including “downsizing” versus “down-sizing” and “up-sampling” versus “upsampling.”
The paper does not empirically evaluate search or final-architecture robustness, for example through architecture-distribution analysis on NASBench-201.
Section 4.1’s second paragraph is missing the articles “the” in its first sentence.
The paper does not provide enough detail about the network architectures to support reproducibility.
The experiments do not evaluate larger datasets such as ImageNet.
It is unclear whether training changes, what loss and training procedure are used, and how samples are generated during training.
Section 4’s analysis appears to assume a deterministic underlying MDP; the assumption is unclear, and the required policy may not exist in stochastic environments.
The paper does not clearly state its motivation.
Section 5.2's claim that in-distribution performance is unchanged is not established because the evaluation cannot identify all truly in-distribution images.
The MNIST-only experiments do not show whether the findings generalize to other, more realistic datasets.
The paper does not adequately discuss or justify its substantial departure from standard worst-case differential privacy to an average-case notion.
Theorem 2 leaves ε unconstrained, making its finite-iteration neighborhood guarantee potentially vacuous; Eq. 21 should establish a bound for arbitrarily small ε.
The paper is poorly written and organized.
Page 2 contains typos.
Experiments use a simplified network and do not assess convolutional, recurrent, or residual layers, leaving behavior across architectures uncertain.
The paper uses abbreviations before defining them and leaves mathematical variables undefined, including on page 5.
The paper does not clarify how Lemma 2 and Theorem 2’s convergence analysis differs from Deshpande et al. [1], particularly for the non-convex setting.
The experiments lack comparisons with existing methods, such as Barceló et al. (ICLR 2020).
The notation reuses h with multiple meanings in Equations (6) and (11).
The experimental section contains minor implementation details that should be moved to the appendix.
Figure 3 lacks x-axis labels.
Section 4.2's update equation may have its tilded and untilded terms reversed, and its relation to the verbal description is unclear.
The Introduction’s claim that prior models show “strong generalization” is subjective and unsupported relative to human generalization.
The paper does not clarify whether it uses the standard miniImageNet split, important for comparison with CAVIA's original-paper results.
The paper does not clarify whether differential quantization applies to both weights and activations or how gradients propagate through quantized activations.
The main paper relegates too much methodological detail and experimental results to the appendix; some should be moved into the main text.
Figure 5 suggests the experiments were not run to convergence, so the reported performance differences may change with full training.
The paper does not explain Equation (6) as gradient descent on a modified loss with a quadratic Δ² term or analyze the resulting Hessian effects, finite-ρ₁ shifts, and ρ₁/ρ₂ decay.
The experiments lack comparisons with more baselines.
The paper does not discuss how its analysis might extend to deep nonlinear networks.
Section 4.1 does not clearly specify its training data relative to Section 4.2’s 10k-sample setup or whether its final paragraph describes a different training regime.
The full-dimensional data assumption leaves the results’ applicability to low-intrinsic-dimension data unclear.
The paper gives no results for applying the method to a trained VAE with a StyleGAN decoder and does not justify its GAN-only focus.
The experiments omit details needed for reproduction, including the learning algorithm, neural-network layout if applicable, and cross-validation used for tuning.
The rightmost Figure 4 plots are difficult to interpret because they are overcrowded and use similar colors.
The evaluation lacks large-scale datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.
The paper does not discuss how tight Theorem 1’s bound is, weakening support for using one approach as a computationally feasible substitute for the other.
The paper uses DQN rather than DDQN without discussing why, despite DDQN’s reduced overestimation bias and BDQN’s DDQN foundation.
Figure 3 does not explain how its results were generated.
Table 2 is not adequately explained.
The paper does not explain why its approach outperforms competing methods.
The paper does not adequately explain how its approach differs from other model-based and adaptive policy-learning methods.
Section 4’s motivation appears to assume independently controllable state features and rescaled offset actions, making its unstructured random-walk model weakly relevant to realistic RL.
The paper lacks a clear related-work section.
The method’s novelty is limited because it mainly combines maximum-entropy RL with value expansion and stochastic value gradients rather than introducing a new model-based modeling approach.
The related-work discussion omits relevant approaches, including Fader Networks and Deep Feature Interpolation.
Several citations are badly formatted; the paper should use citation commands such as \citet and \citep appropriately.
Fig. 1b and the other training curves do not help explain the approach.
Section 3.1 does not clearly specify whether r_i,j denotes one image or a concatenated row, or how input images are arranged as channels or concatenated.
The paper lacks comparisons of effective sparsity across architectures such as convolutional networks and MLPs, which may allocate and prune parameters differently.
The paper does not show whether the proposed method performs well with small batch sizes such as 2, 4, or 8, or explain batch-size effects.
The paper does not rigorously show that the disparity matrix remains full rank throughout training; full rank at initialization would not establish this.
The paper does not clarify its pretraining process.
The paper does not justify its choice of distance metric or compare it with the simpler L2 distance.
The results lack error bars.
The paper does not report how results vary across initialization schemes.
The paper provides no theoretical analysis or guarantee of convergence for the optimization algorithm.
The paper does not explain or substantiate why its model is more generalizable than baseline models.
The references are formatted inconsistently.
The constraint may overrestrict low-dimensional linear function approximation, potentially explaining why Baird's counterexample does not converge to zero.
Table 2 shows only marginal gains, and the method fails to surpass SOTA in several settings.
Section 2.2 refers to a figure that is not cited.
The method’s contribution is incremental compared with earlier work.
The paper does not justify choosing KL divergence over simpler MSE or explain why MSE is incompatible, despite the added complexity in Eqs. 9–11.
The random baseline is inadequate; the paper should compare the model-based approach against its model-free approach.
The paper does not explain how the method behaves on high-dimensional problems.
Figures 1 and 2 are difficult to read because their fonts are too small.
The related-work discussion omits relevant approaches, including LfND, RL with GAN shaping, and Cycle-of-Learning.
Table 1’s bolding is non-intuitive because bold usually indicates the best-performing methods; italics may be clearer.
The experiments do not establish whether the proposed method scales well.
The paper does not clearly position its approach relative to MPO and DistRL.
The experiments lack comparisons with TRPO or DDPG.
Section 2.1 is missing citations.
The experiments do not establish whether gains over related methods come from the proposed approach or stronger neural-network architectures.
The paper has little representation-learning content, making it a poor fit for ICLR.
Section 4's method exposition is too complicated and unclear to understand, even after repeated reading of the main text and appendix.
Section 2.2's weighting strategy and the first equation on page 8 are ad hoc and lack theoretical justification.
Related work omits the closely related study arXiv:1609.04836.
The derivation from the first to the second line of relation (4) is not explained.
Table 2 lacks state-of-the-art methods evaluated under the same setting for demonstrating the model’s effectiveness.
Section 4.1 does not formally define the proposed method for detecting critical substructures.
The Introduction’s second paragraph introduces TPR without explaining why or when it is useful.
Theorem 4.7 is missing an expectation on g(x_a).
Table 1 omits relevant datasets, including Moving MNIST and Robot Pushing.
Section 4.1’s early results rely on the unrealistic assumption that ensemble-member regions and ensemble regions are identical; Proposition 1’s assumptions are too strong.
Figure 3 evaluates planner loss between inferred and true rewards but does not establish whether the algorithm recovers demonstrators’ actual biases.
The value of 2-FGNN is not novel because Maron et al. [1] already demonstrated it.
The notation for OU noise, ${\cal OU}(\mu';\sigma')$, is not introduced.
The experiments do not explain how they empirically justify the paper’s lower bound.
Section 4.4 refers to Table 1 where the reviewer says it should refer to Table 2.
The paper does not provide a complexity analysis of its method.
The paper lacks comparisons against baselines.
The experiments do not report how many random seeds were run.
The paper does not compare its approach with state-of-the-art MTL methods.
The contribution is fairly incremental, extending an existing adaptive-softmax approach to input representations.
Section 2.1 does not explain the proposed architecture clearly enough for non-experts.
The novelty is limited because the paper combines previously proposed combinatorial search and acyclicity-constraint ideas for structure learning.
The paper does not describe how training data are sampled.
Fig. 3 shows substantial performance variation, so it does not establish that either method has converged.
Definition 1 and Section 3.3 leave N undefined.
Section 4.1 does not clearly explain how action and environment information are disentangled and exploited.
The α=2 weight-decay ablation does not establish whether its supposedly stronger, more distinguishable features improve downstream performance.
Some citations are incorrectly formatted in the text.
The attack comparison omits white-box baselines such as PGD and C&W, so it does not establish superiority over standard attacks.
The acknowledgments section violates the double-blind submission policy.
Section 4.3 is missing a space before a comma in its first paragraph.
Tables 1 and 2 are crowded and should be rearranged for readability.
The paper does not explain why retraining improves performance even without pruning, despite the expectation that samples converge to the same minimum.
Page 6 shows accuracy dropping after 20 epochs for both proposed and baseline perturbation methods across three datasets, casting doubt on effectiveness versus random search.
The paper lacks a discussion of limitations of its approach.
The experiments compare only simple models and omit relevant methods such as MXGNet, LEN, Rel-AIR, and SCL.
The paper insufficiently explains how its non-spiking Hodgkin–Huxley model differs from existing spiking SNN models, focusing instead on datasets and accuracy.
Computational cost is not adequately analyzed, including the SVD in Equation (7), per-iteration cost, and the possibility of O(nd) rank-one SVD updates.
The paper omits its tokenization scheme and does not explain how subword tokens are combined into concept representations.
Figure 4 is difficult to assess because of poor rendering and layout, with low- and high-resolution ground-truth images too small for comparison.
The paper does not evaluate the proposed method’s robustness under adversarial attacks.
Experiments are limited to toy problems and do not establish whether the approach improves on prior methods; more complex experiments are needed.
The paper does not report how performance changes with different K values.
The paper’s transductive training setup is a limitation, with no inductive setting addressed.
The claim that the method is highly data efficient compared with existing approaches lacks strong experimental evidence.
The paper does not explain how its method advances the longer-term goal of interpretable representations.
Figure 5 lacks results for longer training episodes on the 5-step tasks.
Table 2 shows limited improvement for the fine-tuned model, which the authors should explain.
The paper does not explain how α is chosen.
The reported improvements are marginal.
The paper does not explain how hyperparameter p should be chosen.
Comparisons may be unfair because prior methods may not be trained under the paper's experimental setting.
The method's applicability is unclear because the model appears restricted to lower-dimensional settings.
The paper does not clearly specify which tasks are considered or how they are generated.
The comparison omits relevant word-embedding post-processing methods, including retrofitting, counter-fitting, and semantic specialization using automatically constructed constraints.
The paper lacks original-image-space visualizations showing whether the learned representations capture visually meaningful concepts.
The paper's 2× learning-rate choice is unexplained and lacks evidence that square-root or linear scaling fails at the full-batch limit.
Table 2 does not identify the best-performing method, making its results confusing.
Figure 3’s results at R=2 differ from Figure 5 without an explanation.
The method’s advantage over expansion-based methods may narrow when using lightweight network architectures.
The practical implementation of the paper’s multi-agent formulation is unclear.
The paper does not clearly explain why its attention blocks produce better results than previous methods; the explanation of residual non-local attention learning in Section 3.3 is vague.

The analysis relies on restrictive, unrealistic assumptions from Mandt et al.; in particular, the Gaussian gradient-noise assumption is not justified by the CLT in the paper’s high-dimensional setting.
Table 2’s baseline results appear insufficiently tuned.
The paper does not explain whether policy-gradient methods offer an advantage over value iteration or policy iteration in its setting.
The paper does not compare its method with other methods.
The Related Works claim that training a model-free policy avoids the usual problem is not explained, since long simulated rollouts from a learned model may still diverge.
The paper does not report the ensemble size used in the experiments.
The paper lacks comparisons with prior approaches, including A3C, DDPG, and TRPO.
The paper lacks side-by-side comparisons with other approaches.
Section 2 assumes correctly labeled training data greatly outnumbers test data without justification, limiting applicability where unlabeled test data is more abundant.
The paper lacks qualitative or ablation analysis of what the teacher actually learns.
Clustering methods usable with the learned representation appear limited to discrete distance measures, but the implications of this limitation are not discussed.
The process for generating the 100,000 training instances and their distribution or patterns is not described, leaving potential dataset limitations unclear.
The paper’s implicit contradiction of Theis et al.’s argument against monolithic generative-model metrics is not sufficiently supported.
The paper does not report the number of test splits or initializations, or standard deviations, so the significance of the accuracy differences is unclear.
The decoder’s 1-D deconvolutions and dimension-wise Bi-LSTMs may overlap in function, and the paper does not justify using both.
The results do not clearly show a benefit over the already strong methods (a) and (b) in Table 1.
The method's better results than the single model are counterintuitive and lack justification against independently trained tasks.
The paper does not clarify which variables are observed and which are latent.
The paper lacks experiments explaining its findings, such as monitoring model parameters or gradients during training.
The paper does not evaluate the approach on different tasks.
Reported results are far below cited state-of-the-art figures, including 5% error and 95.75% accuracy, without explaining the discrepancy.
The evaluation lacks comparisons on additional environments, such as Atari and partially observable DM-Lab or Habitat.
Section 5.1.2 lacks evaluation under subtler, gradual distribution shifts, such as those in Ovadia et al. (2019).
The paper does not theoretically establish that its proposed training method is better than standard SGD.
The results lack error bars or confidence intervals and do not report the number of independent runs.
Several baselines cited in the paper are missing from the experiments, making the roughly 10% gain difficult to compare with the state of the art.
The title suggests general manifold applicability, but the discussion focuses on spherical structures and does not clarify whether the method works for arbitrary topologies.
The experiments are limited to rather small datasets.
Equation (5)'s reward form is insufficiently justified; using average reward for unsafe state-action pairs is not shown to penalize them.
The paper lacks a detailed ablation study.
The choices of T=10 for synthetic data and T=3 for real-world data appear ad hoc and are not justified or validated.
The paper does not explain under what conditions its reward augmentation improves or worsens outcomes, and provides no formal theory.
Generating the training data appears to require exponential computation, making the proposed approach difficult to use in practice.
The claimed sample-complexity improvement over prior work overlooks [3]’s dependence on the minimum of task and state counts and [4]’s dependence on transition templates.
The paper does not examine the geometry of the learned representations.
The paper does not explain the motivation for combining the techniques or why their combination should work.
The paper does not clearly state the assumptions or conditions under which its attacks are valid, making the threat setting difficult to assess.
The image tasks’ 2D layout may supply an architectural inductive bias, making the value of their regular long-range correspondences as benchmark targets unclear.
The evaluation metric is not explained sufficiently.
The paper does not evaluate whether the method scales to more classes or more complex datasets.
The paper does not compare language-modeling performance against standard LSTMs.
The overall algorithm combines heuristics without a principled derivation, leaving its design rationale insufficiently grounded.
The paper does not explain why enumeration-based approaches would fail to synthesize these programs.
Section 4.2.2 claims compositionality despite low refdis without a rigorous qualitative explanation, weakening the metric’s usefulness.
The paper does not explain its 3D point-cloud focus despite the method’s applicability to 2D and a small 2D experiment.
The reported scores do not establish conditional language-generation quality; the paper lacks BLEU or another suitable metric.
The evaluation lacks additional datasets for a more rigorous benchmark.
The tables omit training and inference times, so the method’s speed relative to its baselines is unclear.
The experiments do not convincingly show an advantage over Uncertainty or SGBS, which perform well in some cases.
The experiments do not demonstrate scalability beyond the largest tested graph of about 5K nodes, despite the complexity discussion in Table 1 and Section A.5.
The paper insufficiently motivates robustness to large L∞ perturbations, which may cause perceptual changes above 16/255 and where CW-L2 may be more appropriate.
The paper does not report how the approach affects training time.
Experiments omit comparisons with the learning-curve method [1] and [Wilson et al., 2016].
The experiments do not test whether reordering also improves the 2-way prototypical model, making it difficult to isolate the one-way proposal’s gain.
The paper does not discuss the statistical significance of its results.
The paper does not evaluate its claimed computational-time benefits.
The experiments use word-based systems rather than state-of-the-art subword models, leaving it unclear whether the conclusions generalize.
The paper does not use a standard evaluation methodology, making its results difficult to interpret.
The paper does not report how sensitive results are to hyperparameter values.
The paper provides no ablation study.
The approach requires a large number of CPUs, raising concerns about its computational cost and scalability.
The evaluation covers too few application areas to establish that the enhancements generalize across a wide variety of tasks or can broadly replace traditional baselines.
The evaluation lacks standard image-quality metrics such as FID or a related measure.
Section A.2 shows the method is incompatible with federated averaging, limiting its practical use under communication bottlenecks.
The evaluation lacks clear baseline comparisons, including comparisons with naive alternatives.
